problem: Existing audio-visual navigation (AVN) work targets single agents and cannot exploit multi-agent coordination, which matters in time-sensitive settings such as emergency response. There is no scalable multi-agent AVN platform or model.
motivation: Multiple agents starting from different positions cover more area and can fuse multimodal information via implicit interaction, which should raise success rate and cut completion time. Prior multi-agent RL work is mostly visual and does not address audio-visual navigation.
key_idea: Treat the joint audio-visual observations of several agents as a sequence and process them with a MAT-inspired multi-encoder plus shared-decoder Transformer (MAST) that gives each agent a temporal state representation for its own actor-critic.
insight: The ablations show that both the per-agent modality encoders and the shared decoder are needed. On Replica, removing the encoders (w/o EN) drops Heard SR from 99.9 to 76.2, and removing the decoder (w/o DE) drops it to 70.9; Unheard SR falls from 72.4 to 46.3 and 39.5. The decoder, which carries the cross-agent interaction, matters most. However, the comparison against single-agent baselines is confounded, since the metrics come from whichever of the two agents finishes first.
method: Patch embedding: egocentric visual and audio (binaural) inputs are turned into embedding vectors.
Per-agent modality encoders: separate visual and audio Transformer encoder blocks (self-attention, MLP, residual) produce information sequences I and B for each agent.
Joint state observation: the sequences of all agents are concatenated into C_t=(I1,B1,I2,B2,...).
Shared decoder: a multi-head attention decoder processes C_t autoregressively, so each agent sees the earlier agents' observations and states, and outputs a temporal state representation per agent.
Actor-critic heads: a single linear layer each for policy and value per agent; trained with actor+critic+entropy loss averaged over agents.
Reward: +10 when the first agent reaches the goal and stops, +0.25 for reducing Manhattan distance to the target, -0.01 time penalty per action per agent.
Scalability: more agents are handled by adding encoders and extending the decoder sequence length/dimension.

setting.backbone: Custom Transformer encoder-decoder (MAST) trained from scratch with actor-critic RL
setting.training_data: RL in SoundSpaces dual-agent environments: 40M steps on Replica, 60M steps on Matterport3D
setting.observation: egocentric RGB visual + binaural audio per agent
setting.action_space: discrete low-level actions on the SoundSpaces grid (500 step limit per agent)
setting.privileged: none stated (Manhattan distance to the target is used in the training reward)

numbers.extra: Two agents; metrics taken from the agent that finishes first

numbers_note: The paper does not name splits; the SoundSpaces test protocol is assumed, and Heard/Unheard are reported as separate rows. The benchmarks are not in the canonical list, so they are named 'other:'.
results: With two agents, MAST-AVN beats the strongest single-agent baseline ORAN on Replica by +3.2 SR (Heard) and +11.5 SR (Unheard), and beats AV-WaN on Matterport3D by +5.3 and +16.5 SR. It also beats a naive two-agent AV-Nav (Replica Unheard SR 72.4 vs 59.9; Matterport3D Unheard SR 73.2 vs 50.1).
limitations: Comparisons with single-agent baselines are unfair because the metrics come from whichever of two agents finishes first.
Only implicit communication and only two agents are evaluated; the claimed scalability to more agents is not tested.
Ablations are limited to removing the encoders or the decoder; no simulator-independent or real-robot validation.
